text:
In the Provincial Court of Alberta

Citation: Condominium
Corporation No 8722942 v Buck, 2019 ABPC 305

Date:
20191205

Docket:
P1890300081

Registry:
Edmonton

Between:

Condominium Corporation No 8722942

Plaintiff

- and -

Jon Buck and Sandra Gaviria-Buck

Defendants

Reasons for Decision of the
Honourable
Judge

S.L. Corbett

I.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The Plaintiff, Condominium Corporation No. 8722942 (“Oakwood Towers”),
sues Jon Buck (“Mr. Buck”) and Sandra Gaviria Buck (“Mrs. Buck”).  Mr. and Mrs.
Buck (“the Bucks” collectively) were Oakwood Towers’ resident property managers
from May 1, 2014 until July 31, 2016
[1]
.
Oakwood Towers is a condominium property located in Edmonton, AB.

[
2
]

Oakwood Towers says that the Bucks fraudulently paid themselves vacation
pay on termination.  Oakwood Towers seeks repayment of $8,094.00.

[
3
]

The Bucks counter sue Oakwood Towers claiming that Oakwood Towers
breached the Management Agreement (“the Agreement”) between them by wrongfully
terminating the Agreement, and dismissing the Bucks from their positions as
Managers of the Oakwood Towers condominium property.  The Bucks filed separate
Dispute Notes and Counterclaims, which make substantially the same
allegations.  The Bucks seek $50,000.00 each.

[
4
]

Oakwood Towers defends the Counterclaims on the basis that the Bucks
were “insubordinate”, and that the Bucks were terminated as a result of that
insubordination pursuant to Section 13 of the Agreement.

[
5
]

I raised a jurisdictional question at the outset of the 4 day trial,
asking for counsel’s input on whether this action would engage the
Condominium
Property Act
[2]

as the
Act
defines the “Court” as the “Court of Queen’s Bench of
Alberta”, and as the Provincial Court of Alberta only enjoys concurrent
jurisdiction with Queen’s Bench with respect to Section 36 matters.  Otherwise,
and in particular, with respect to Section 67 matters, this Court has no
jurisdiction.
[3]

Counsel assured me that this action would not engage
Section 67
of the
Act
,
and we proceeded with the trial on that basis.

[
6
]

The Bucks’ lawyer advised he had instructions from the Bucks to withdraw
the Bucks’ claims for aggravated damages, and accordingly, no evidence was
called on that issue.  These Reasons will not address the Bucks’ aggravated
damages claims based on the Bucks’ withdrawals.

II.

ISSUES

Oakwood Towers’ Action against the Bucks
:

Whether the Bucks fraudulently
paid themselves vacation pay on termination?

A.        Introduction

B.        Whether the Bucks were entitled to
vacation pay under the Agreement?

C.        What vacations
did the Bucks taken between May, 2014 and July, 2016?  Did the Bucks use up
their entire vacation time as alleged by Oakwood Towers?

D.        What is the
appropriate calculation of the vacation pay that the Bucks were entitled to
upon termination of the Agreement?

E.         How was the
vacation pay paid to the Bucks?  Specifically, what was the process that was
followed to review, approve and issue the Bucks’ vacation pay cheques?  Was
vacation pay paid wrongfully to the Bucks?

F.         Was vacation pay paid
fraudulently to the Bucks?

G.        What are the
legal elements of civil fraud?  Has Oakwood Towers proven, on a balance of
probabilities, that the Bucks were guilty of civil fraud in relation to payment
of the vacation pay?

H.        Conclusion

Bucks’ Action against Oakwood Towers:

Whether Oakwood Towers properly terminated
the Management Agreement with the Bucks on the basis that the Bucks were
insubordinate?

A.        What were the terms of the
Agreement regarding termination?

B.        What was the basis on which
Oakwood Towers terminated the Agreement?

C.        Did the
Agreement create an employment relationship between Oakwood Towers and the Bucks?

D.        Who bears the onus of proof?

E.         Were the Bucks individual
employees?

F.         What is just cause, and how is it
determined at law?

G.        What is insubordination?

H.        Were the Bucks
insubordinate?  Were there cumulative minor acts of insubordination that justified
termination of the Agreement?  Was there one pivotal act of insubordination
that justified termination of the Agreement?

1.         September
1, 2015 – Board Meeting

2.         December,
2015 – Stenzel Suite Management Agreement

3.         January,
2016 – Roofing Invoice and Reserve Fund Transfer

4.         June,
2016 – Reserve Fund Annual Report

5.         July,
2016 – Cease and Desist Direction (the alleged “pivotal act”)

I.          Was the notice of termination
inconsistent with just cause?

J.          Were the
Bucks insubordinate, or was only Mr. Buck insubordinate?  If Mr. Buck, not Mrs.
Buck, was insubordinate, what effect does that have on Oakwood Towers’
termination of the Agreement for insubordination?

K.        Conclusion

What damages are the Bucks entitled to for
wrongful termination of the Agreement?

A.        As the
Agreement was a fixed term contract, were the Bucks under any duty to mitigate
their damages?  Was there any evidence of any mitigation principles which might
assist Oakwood Towers?

B.        What is the appropriate
calculation of Mr. and Mrs. Buck’s damages?

C.        Are the
separate Counterclaims filed by Mr. and Mrs. Buck independent actions?  Do each
of Mr. and Mrs. Buck have independent actions against Oakwood Towers for
wrongful termination of the Agreement?

D.        Conclusion

Both Actions:

Whether the Bucks are entitled to party and
party costs, enhanced costs or solicitor-client costs?

OAKWOOD TOWERS’ ACTION AGAINST THE BUCKS:

III.

WHETHER THE BUCKS FRAUDULENTLY PAID THEMSELVES VACATION PAY ON
TERMINATION?

A.

Introduction

[
7
]

Oakwood Towers’ Civil Claim alleges that, “the Bucks paid themselves,
terminated property managers, funds fraudulently”.  The Civil Claim was filed
on behalf of Oakwood Towers by its corporate representative, Natasha Stenzel
(“Stenzel”).

[
8
]

Oakwood Towers appeared to soften this position at the outset of the trial
suggesting that the Bucks were not entitled to the vacation pay that they were
paid.  In written argument, Oakwood Towers argued that the Bucks “wrongfully
paid themselves $8,094.00 in unearned vacation pay”.

B.

Entitlement to Vacation Pay

[
9
]

The Agreement, in Section 10, entitled the Bucks to take three weeks
paid vacation per year.  The Bucks were further entitled to carry over unused
vacation time.

[
10
]

At the time of Oakwood Towers’ termination of the Agreement
[4]
, Section 8 of
the Agreement set out a gross monthly salary of $6,025.00 per month.
[5]

[
11
]

There is no question, based on the Agreement, that the Bucks were
entitled to paid vacation based on the Agreement between Oakwood Towers and the
Bucks.

[
12
]

In argument, counsel for the Bucks referred me to
Sections 34
to
44
of
the
Employment Standards Code
[6]
,
in further support of the Bucks’ entitlement to vacation pay on termination.
Section 42(2) sets out that an employer must pay out vacation pay on
termination of employment.
[7]

[
13
]

Oakwood Towers did not dispute the Bucks’ contractual entitlement to
paid vacation, or the legislated entitlement to vacation pay on termination.

[
14
]

I find that the Bucks were entitled to be paid vacation pay on
termination pursuant to the Agreement and pursuant to the
Employment
Standards Code
.
[8]

C.

Vacation Time Taken by the Bucks

[
15
]

Mrs. Buck testified that she and Mr. Buck took one vacation between May,
2014 and their termination in July, 2016.  Specifically, they went to Florida
from Monday, May 18, 2015 to Monday, May 25
[9]
,
2015.  The Bucks produced their Air Miles Travel Confirmation confirming their
flight itinerary for their Florida vacation in addition to an email to Oakwood
Towers board members confirming their itinerary, advising they would be leaving
Monday, May 18 and returning to work “Wednesday, May 27, 2015”
[10]
.  Mrs. Buck advised the board
that she would notify the accountants of their vacation.  When the Bucks
returned on Tuesday, May 26, 2015, Mrs. Buck sent a text message to Stenzel
confirming their return from vacation earlier that day, outlining the work she
had done that day, and confirming that she had taken the telephone off call
forwarding.

[
16
]

Mrs. Buck was not cross-examined by Oakwood Towers on her evidence.
[11]

[
17
]

Stenzel was Oakwood Towers’ corporate representative in this Action.
Stenzel claimed that the Bucks “were paid in full” while on vacation, and that
the Bucks’ vacations “were well-documented”
[12]
.

[
18
]

Despite Stenzel’s assertion that the Bucks’ vacations “were
well-documented”, the only documented vacation was the Bucks’ vacation to
Florida of 5 working days in May, 2015.  Stenzel claimed that the Bucks
returned on May 27, 2015 as opposed to May 26, 2015.  I find that the Bucks
returned from their Florida vacation on May 26, 2015, not May 27, and that they
took the 5 working days vacation that Mrs. Buck attested to.

[
19
]

Stenzel testified that the Bucks took 4 days off in January, 2015,
without specifically identifying the dates.  She further testified that the
Bucks “took off a great deal of extra days on a front side of and back side of
a weekend”, commenting they took “numerous little days” off.  She repeated that
they had a “lot of time off”, and that “they took in excess of their allotted
six weeks in total vacations” during their tenure as Oakwood Towers’ managers.

[
20
]

Oakwood Towers’ board minutes from April 12, 2016 set out that the
“board approved October 28 to November 11, 2016” as vacation for management.
Stenzel was not asked why Oakwood Towers approved further vacation time if the
Bucks had indeed used in excess of their allotted vacation during their tenure.
Oakwood Towers provided no explanation for why it approved the Bucks’ 2016
proposed vacation, if the Bucks had no vacation time left.

[
21
]

Stenzel was cross-examined about whether Oakwood Towers had any records
of the Bucks’ “well-documented” vacations.  Stenzel referred to the air travel
confirmation referred to in Paragraph 15 in response to that question, in
addition to repeating that the Bucks “took a great deal of time off”.
Stenzel was not able to refer to any other records of Oakwood Towers of
vacations taken by the Bucks, despite Oakwood Towers’ allegation that the
Bucks’ “vacations were well documented”.  Instead, Stenzel asserted that the
Bucks should have supplied Oakwood Towers with a list of time they took off.

[
22
]

Oakwood Towers relies on Stenzel’s evidence to argue that the Bucks were
not entitled to the full $8,094.00 vacation pay.  This argument turns on Stenzel’s
evidence that the Bucks took more vacation days than the 5 working days
documented.

[
23
]

Stenzel’s evidence differed from that of Mrs. Buck and from the
documentary evidence entered at Trial.  This requires me to assess both
credibility and reliability.  The factors to be considered in assessing
credibility include witness demeanour, memory, plausibility, internal
consistency, external consistency, motivation and ability to perceive.
[13]

[
24
]

Reliability and credibility are distinct.  Reliability relates to the
witness’ ability to accurately observe, recall and recount the events in
issue.  Credibility relates to the witness’ sincerity, that is, his or her
willingness to speak the truth as the witness believes it to be.
[14]
Internal
consistency relates to whether the witness’ evidence is consistent with past
statements as well as evidence remaining consistent throughout testimony.
External consistency relates to whether the witness’ evidence is consistent
with external facts established by other witnesses or by documentary evidence.
[15]

[
25
]

Stenzel’s evidence was inconsistent with Mrs. Buck’s evidence and with
the documentary evidence.  Her evidence that the Bucks took additional vacation
time lacked precision in terms of the exact number of days, and the specific
dates.  Oakwood Towers was the Bucks’ employer
[16]
,
and Oakwood Towers was statutorily obliged to keep records of the Bucks’
vacations showing start and finish dates and the period of employment in which
the annual vacation was earned
[17]
.

[
26
]

Contrary to Stenzel’s assertion, it was not the Bucks’ responsibility to
provide Oakwood Towers with records of their vacations.  Stenzel was unable to
refer to any other records of vacations taken by the Bucks apart from those
referred to in Paragraph 15.   Oakwood Towers, through its corporate
representative Stenzel, failed to produce any records of the Bucks’ vacation
time as required by the
Employment Standards Code
[18]
.
Stenzel filed the Civil Claim on behalf of Oakwood Towers alleging “fraud”, and
as will be discussed later in these Reasons, Stenzel had a conflict with the
Bucks unrelated to the Agreement.  This calls into question Stenzel’s
motivation.  I find Stenzel’s evidence, on behalf of Oakwood Towers, to be
vague, imprecise and unreliable on this issue, even without taking into account
Oakwood Towers’ failure to cross examine Mrs. Buck on this issue.

[
27
]

Based on the evidence, I accept Mrs. Buck’s evidence, and I find that
the Bucks took 5 working days vacation between May, 2014 and July, 2016.
Stenzel’s evidence on this issue was not reliable for the reasons outlined in Paragraphs
25 and 26.   Oakwood Towers offered no reliable evidence substantiating that
the Bucks took more than 5 working days of vacation between May, 2014 and July,
2016.

D.

Calculation of Vacation Pay

[
28
]

Upon receiving Oakwood Tower’s letter dated July 15, 2016 terminating
the Agreement, Mr. Buck reached out to Darren Kam (“Kam”), Oakwood Towers’
accountant
[19]
,
by email on July 20, 2016.

[
29
]

Mr. Buck advised Kam that he and Mrs. Buck had taken 5 working days of
vacation, and that they were entitled to 3 weeks paid vacation per year and to
carry over unused vacation time.  Mr. Buck attached a copy of the Agreement.
Mr. Buck asked a specific question about the Bucks’ entitlement to be paid in
lieu for vacation.  Kam responded to Mr. Buck asking whether the board approved
pay out for unused vacation.  Mr. Buck responded to Kam indicating that he had
called Employment Standards
[20]
,
and had “confirmed” that “there is no requirement for board approval” for a
pay-out of unused vacation.  Mr. Buck then told Kam that their employment was
ending at the end of July, 2016, and “so by law”, they were “entitled to be
paid out for unused vacation time”.  He invited Kam to contact Employment
Standards, and provided a number for him to call.  Kam told Mr. Buck that he
sent the request for the calculation to his office’s “programmers”, and was
waiting for a response.

[
30
]

Kam provided Mr. Buck with a Vacation Pay calculation on July 29, 2016.
Mr. Buck asked Kam what the next steps were that they needed to take, or was “everything
good to go”.  Specifically, he asked Kam if they could print off Kam’s
calculation, and write cheques for Mr. Buck for $4,332.66 and for Mrs. Buck for
$3,761.34, and have the board members with signing authority sign off on the
cheques as per normal with all other cheques that they write.  In the
alternative, Mr. Buck asked Kam whether they needed to “follow another kind of
process”.  Kam responded that he would print it off and “show it to the board”,
admitting he did not know what the “process” was as he was not a “payroll
expert”.

[
31
]

Kam testified that he recommended that the Bucks show the Vacation Pay
calculation to the board because the board was “technically” his firm’s
client.  He “assumed” that the next step would be for the Vacation Pay calculation
to be approved by the board.  He acknowledged that was his “understanding”
based on “what he thought should be done”.  Kam admitted that he had no
information on what the process was.

[
32
]

The Vacation Pay calculation was produced, and no evidence was called to
suggest that the calculation of the Bucks’ vacation pay of $4,332.66 for Mr.
Buck and $3,761.34 for Mrs. Buck, based on the 5 working days of vacation they
took in May, 2015, was not accurate.  I have already addressed and dismissed
Stenzel’s evidence that the Bucks took their full vacation entitlement between
May, 2014 and July, 2016.

[
33
]

I find that the calculation of Vacation Pay as provided by Kam to the
Bucks was accurate.

E.

Payment of Vacation Pay

[
34
]

After the Bucks received Kam’s calculation of Vacation Pay, Mr. Buck
presented cheques payable to himself and Mrs. Buck along with the Vacation Pay
calculation to two board members for review and approval.  Oakwood Towers
complains that the cheques issued to the Bucks for vacation pay were only
signed by one board member as opposed to two board members, alleging this was
contrary to a February, 2016 board policy.  Oakwood Towers further accuses the
Bucks of “fraudulently” or “wrongfully” “paying themselves” vacation pay as the
Bucks prepared the cheques for the board members’ approval.

[
35
]

Although Oakwood Towers had approved a policy of requiring two
signatures on all cheques on February 9, 2016, that policy was not followed
between February and July, 2016 while the Bucks were the Oakwood Towers’
managers.

[
36
]

Instead, Oakwood Towers designated board members, Stacey Bigelow
(“Bigelow”)
[21]

and Linda Roberge (“Roberge”), as the two board members responsible for
reviewing and approving invoices, and for signing cheques to pay Oakwood
Towers’ bills.  Each invoice had to be approved by the two board members, and
those two board members were to initial each of the invoices, although only
Roberge generally signed the cheques.

[
37
]

Stenzel was also Oakwood Towers’ Treasurer.   She insisted that board
policy and practice required two board members’ signatures on each cheque
written on behalf of Oakwood Towers.
[22]

Stenzel was responsible for ordering cheques from Oakwood Towers’ bank that had
two signature lines instead of only one to put the new policy into effect.
Although Stenzel testified that she ordered the two signature line cheques from
the bank in February, 2016 to comply with the new policy, the minutes of
Oakwood Towers’ board meeting on March 8, 2016 set out that the “cheques are
going to be ordered”.   The minutes of the board meeting on April 12, 2016 set
out that the board discussed “ordering new cheques”, and the Treasurer
“confirmed an appointment has been made this month with the bank to get
everything set-up”.

[
38
]

Bank statements of Oakwood Towers from February 1, 2016 to July 31, 2016
were put to Stenzel in cross-examination.  Those bank statements attached
cheques paying various invoices on behalf of Oakwood Towers.  There was not a
single cheque attached to those bank statements with more than one signature on
it.  There was not a single cheque with a double signature line – each cheque
only had a single signature line.

[
39
]

Roberge also testified.  Roberge was one of two board members,
designated by Oakwood Towers to have cheque signing authority.

[
40
]

Roberge confirmed the process of paying Oakwood Towers’ bills summarized
in Paragraph 36.  The Bucks would prepare cheques.  The Bucks would attach the
invoices that matched up with the cheques.  Bigelow and Roberge would review
the invoices and cheques for accuracy, and they would both initial each invoice
after review.  Roberge then signed the cheques, and returned the completed
package to the Bucks so the cheques could be mailed out.

[
41
]

I am satisfied based on Mr. Buck’s and Roberge’s evidence that the board
delegated review and approval of Oakwood Towers’ invoices to Roberge and
Bigelow.  In the absence of two signature line cheques, Roberge and Bigelow
followed the board policy of initialing each invoice to indicate approval, and
Roberge alone generally signed the one signature line cheques to pay Oakwood
Towers’ bills between February and July 31, 2016.  I reject Stenzel’s evidence
on the two signature practice as her evidence was inconsistent with that of
Roberge and Mrs. Buck, and with the bank statements produced at trial.

[
42
]

Stenzel’s complaint that the board’s two signature policy was not
followed with respect to the two vacation pay cheques issued to the Bucks, and
for that matter, with any of Oakwood Towers’ cheques from February to July,
2016 ought to have been directed at her fellow board members, not the Bucks
[23]
.

[
43
]

In accordance with the established practice, the Bucks presented cheques
payable to themselves along with the Vacation Pay calculation to Bigelow and
Roberge for review, approval and signature.  While testifying, Roberge reviewed
and confirmed that both her initials and those of Bigelow appear on the
Vacation Pay calculation prepared by Kam which was entered into evidence.
Roberge further confirmed that her signature appears on the two cheques dated
July 29, 2016 payable to the Bucks from Oakwood Towers for their vacation
payout.  The practice which was followed for review and approval of the
vacation pay cheques payable to the Bucks is the same practice that Roberge and
Bigelow had adopted for payment of all of Oakwood Towers’ expenses.  There was
no evidence that something improper occurred.  If Roberge and Bigelow had an
issue with review and approval of the Bucks’ vacation pay, they were positioned
as the designated signing authorities for the board to raise that issue at the
time that the expenses were presented for review and approval.  The Bucks did
not “pay themselves” vacation pay.  Oakwood Towers paid them vacation pay after
the two designated board members followed the process that Oakwood Towers put
into place for review and approval of all expenses.  There was no evidence that
this payment was “wrongful”, or as will be discussed, “fraudulent”.

[
44
]

Stenzel raised three further issues regarding the Bucks’ vacation pay.
Firstly, she testified that there was a board policy which required a board
discussion about the Bucks’ entitlement to vacation pay.  She testified that
the Bucks would have been allowed input into this discussion.  Oakwood Towers
also appeared to rely on Kam’s recommendation that the Bucks show the Vacation
Pay calculation to the board.  Kam admitted he did not know what the process
was, and confessed that he made that recommendation as the board was his
client.  No records of any such policy were entered into evidence.  Oakwood
Towers produced no records, as required by the
Employment Standards Code
[24]
, of the
Bucks’ vacation time, beyond those produced by the Bucks.  As employees, the
Bucks had both a contractual right and a legislative right to payment of their
vacation pay.  Even if Oakwood Towers had produced a board policy corroborating
Stenzel’s testimony, Stenzel’s evidence does not assist Oakwood Towers’
position as there is nothing wrongful about being paid for something you are
entitled to at law.  As an employer, Oakwood Towers was required by law to pay
out vacation pay, irrespective of whether the board wanted to discuss it.

[
45
]

Secondly, Stenzel complained that the Bucks took the cheques to Roberge
and Bigelow for review and approval, contrary to Oakwood Towers Stavropoulos’
direction not to communicate further with the board, owners or residents,
suppliers or contractors.

[
46
]

Stavropoulos’ direction was not as characterized by Stenzel.  Further, the
Bucks were asked to cooperate, and to be positive and helpful during the
transition period between the termination letter of July 15, 2016, and their last
day on July 31, 2016.  The July 31, 2016 bank statement evidences that the
Bucks paid Oakwood Towers’ expenses to the end of the month so they discharged
their duties during the transition period as requested
[25]
.

[
47
]

Thirdly, Stenzel suggested, as did Oakwood Towers in written argument,
that there was a “qualitative” difference between the purpose of the vacation
pay cheques payable to the Bucks and cheques issued for the other day-to-day
expenses of Oakwood Towers.  Oakwood Towers argues that the Bucks should have made
greater effort to comply with the board two signature policy on cheques payable
to themselves.  I have carefully reviewed the one signature line cheques
attached to Oakwood Towers’ bank statements for the period February 1 to July
31, 2016
[26]
.
Prior to the July 29, 2016 vacation cheques, the Bucks had received a total of
23 cheques from Oakwood Towers, including monthly pay cheques all in exactly
the same way (ie. with one signature line and following the approval process
described by Roberge).  There was no evidence that there was any “qualitative”
difference, as argued by Oakwood Towers, between the vacation pay cheques and
all the other cheques that had been provided to the Bucks and other payees from
February to July, 2016 (including Mr. Buck’s monthly pay cheques).  Again, if
Bigelow and Roberge had concerns with approval of the vacation cheques, they
were positioned to deny approval of the same.

F.

Allegations of Fraud

[
48
]

On November 15, 2017, more than 16 months after the Bucks’ Agreement was
terminated, Oakwood Towers sent a letter to the Bucks alleging that they owed
$8,094.00, and stating that they “were paid in full” while on vacation, and
that “these vacations were well-documented”.  Oakwood Towers complained that
the cheques issued for the Bucks’ vacation pay only showed one signature, and
that was contrary to a policy passed by the Board in February, 2016.  The
letter stated that the Bucks “not only wrote the cheques in the amounts [they]
were never entitled to but [they] cashed with only one signature”.  The letter
further stated: “This could be deemed as a fraudulent action and criminal
charges can be brought forward.”
[27]

Oakwood Towers then demanded repayment of the sum of $8094.00.

[
49
]

The Bucks’ letter in response is dated December 20, 2017.  Their letter
makes reference to the Agreement that entitled them to take paid vacation and
to carry over unused vacation time.  The Bucks advised Oakwood Towers that they
took only five days’ vacation, and that they received confirmation from the
accountant of their compiled vacation pay entitlement.  The Bucks noted that
the board had not put the two signature requirement into effect as at July 31,
2016. Further, both Roberge and Bigelow reviewed and approved the issuance of
the vacation pay cheques, thereby meeting the requirement of two board members
authorizing the transaction.  The Bucks stated that they were entitled to the
vacation pay issued, and that the cheques in question were issued pursuant to
board’s practice and with the required authorization.

G.

Elements of Civil Fraud

[
50
]

In its demand letter of November, 2017, and in its Civil Claim, Oakwood
Towers insisted that the Bucks “fraudulently” paid themselves vacation pay.

[
51
]

Oakwood Towers bears the onus of proving civil fraud
[28]
.  Civil fraud requires
that Oakwood Towers establish the elements of civil fraud or deceit.  Those
include:

•

A false representation made by the defendant;

•

Some level of knowledge of the falsehood of the representation on
the part of the part defendant (whether through knowledge or recklessness);

•

The false representation caused the plaintiff to act; and

•

The plaintiff’s action resulted in a loss.
[29]

[
52
]

Oakwood Towers, in its written argument, stated that it was “unclear
whether the legal requirements for fraud have been met here”.   Despite that
statement, Oakwood Towers did not seek to amend its Civil Claim that clearly
alleged civil fraud, and Oakwood Towers continued to insist at trial that the
Bucks were guilty of civil fraud.

[
53
]

I have carefully reviewed the evidence.  There was no evidence that the
Bucks made a “false representation” to Oakwood Towers.  They were both
contractually and statutorily entitled to vacation pay.  They asked Oakwood
Towers’ accountant Kam to calculate the vacation pay.  The Bucks provided
evidence of the vacation time they took while managing Oakwood Towers.  Oakwood
Towers failed to produce any reliable evidence calling into question the
accuracy of the vacation records submitted by the Bucks.  The Bucks presented
information they received from Oakwood Towers’ accountant calculating their
entitlement to vacation pay to Oakwood Towers’ designated board members,
Roberge and Bigelow, for review and approval.  Oakwood Towers called no
evidence challenging the accountant’s calculation of vacation pay so there was
no evidence that the calculations presented were false or inaccurate.  The
designated board members reviewed the accountant’s vacation pay calculations,
both initialed the same, and Roberge signed the vacation pay cheques in
accordance with the practice that she and Bigelow adopted, in the absence of
Oakwood Towers providing two signature line cheques for use.    There was no
evidence that the Bucks caused Oakwood Towers to act.  Oakwood Towers, further,
did not sustain any loss from paying the Bucks the vacation pay which they were
entitled to both contractually and statutorily.

[
54
]

Oakwood Towers’ board President John Stavropoulos (“Stavropoulos”)
confirmed there was “no fraud” on the Bucks’ part when he spoke to a Service
Canada representative on September 12, 2016
[30]
.
Stavropoulos further confirmed the accuracy of the information contained in the

[36]

F.

Just Cause Generally

[
76
]

Just cause “is so-called because any cause will not do”
[42]
.  The employee’s alleged
misconduct must be serious enough to repudiate the employment contract such
that the employer is relieved from its common law obligation to provide either
reasonable notice or pay in lieu thereof
[43]
.
“Cause is established where the employee misconduct amounts to a breakdown in
the employment relationship – misconduct that so fractures the relationship to
the point that the employer is not expected to give the employee a second
chance”.
[44]

[
77
]

The question of whether the alleged misconduct constitutes just cause
for termination is determined using a contextual approach.
[45]
Mere proof of
misconduct does not automatically constitute cause.
[46]
The question is whether
the behaviour is such that the employment relationship can no longer viably
exist.
[47]

[
78
]

The
McKinley
[48]

analysis requires that cause be assessed following a 3 step framework:

1.         Determine the nature and extent of the misconduct;

2.         Consider the surrounding circumstances, including
the employment history, the employee’s role and responsibilities, the type of
business or activity, the policies and practices, and the level of trust
reposed in the employee; and

3.         Determine if the response to the proven misconduct
is balanced.  Is the proven misconduct so incompatible with the fundamental
terms of the employment relationship that it warrants dismissal?
[49]

[
79
]

Cause is a question of fact, and is determined by an objective,
contextual and proportional analysis.
[50]

G.

Insubordination

[
80
]

The specific misconduct alleged by Oakwood Towers is insubordination.
Insubordination broadly includes “any refusal … to follow instructions, and any
other conduct … that constitutes a challenge to persons in authority or their
policies”.
[51]

Insubordination has been defined as refusing to obey an order from a person in
authority.
[52]

[
81
]

Insubordination, unlike disobedience, focuses on “concepts concerned
with rudeness or provocative behavior towards the employer”
[53]
.  The same principles
which apply to disobedience apply to insubordination.  In addition, the
following factors are applicable: (1) is the behavior a deliberate challenge?;
(2) generally, two or more instances of insolence or insubordination are
required; (3) if the employee has a reasonable excuse, such as provocation,
this will excuse the misconduct; (4) if the insolent conduct results from an
ongoing personality clash, it may not constitute cause; (5) another factor to
consider is whether there is an apology; (6) the context of the challenge must
also be examined; and  (7) the gravity of the offence must be examined.
[54]

[
82
]

One act of insubordination will not normally be sufficient to justify
termination.
[55]

One act of insubordination may constitute just cause for termination if:

a)

it is grave;

b)

it consists of willful and deliberate disobedience of an order
[56]
;

c)

work rules were made known to the employee;

d)

work rules were consistently enforced;

e)

work rules were clearly communicated to the employee;

f)

the work order was authorized (ie. it came within the scope of the
worker’s duties);

g)

the worker was made aware unequivocally that discipline is the penalty
for disobedience

h)

the work order was lawful and reasonable;

i)

the employee had no reasonable excuse for disobedience;

j)

the breach was serious.

[
83
]

All of the above factors are not necessarily required to make a finding
of insubordination.  The court must assess all relevant circumstances to
determine if insubordination justified termination.
[57]

[
84
]

Usually one instance of insubordination will not be sufficient to
warrant dismissal.
[58]

The cumulative effect of a number of minor instances of misconduct may, in some
circumstances, justify dismissal.
[59]

The series of incidents must equate to a deterioration in the parties’
relationship, and the conduct “must go to the heart of the employment
contract”.
[60]

Cumulative cause for dismissal requires that the employer prove that the
employee was given express and clear warnings; the employee was given a
reasonable opportunity to improve his/her performance after the warning;
notwithstanding the foregoing, the employee failed to improve; and the
cumulative failings would prejudice the employer’s business.
[61]

[
85
]

“Willful disobedience” has been defined as “defiance by an employee of a
lawful and reasonable order that effectively repudiates the essential condition
of the employment relationship”.
[62]

The order must either be clear and specific or a breach of policies and
procedures well known by the employee; within the scope of the employee’s job
duties; reasonable and lawful; and involving some matter of import.
[63]
The
disobedience must be both deliberate and intentional rather than an honest
mistake or a reasonable belief that s/he was not disobeying; unless the act of
disobedience is particularly serious it has to be repeated, rather than be
isolated to constitute cause.
[64]

The employer must prove that the disobedience damaged the relationship so that
it could not be carried on, and that the employee understood or should have
understood that s/he ran the risk of termination for disobeying the order.  If
there is a reasonable explanation for the disobedience, it will not be cause
for termination.
[65]

Insubordination will constitute cause where the employer can establish that the
employee willfully violated a clear and unequivocal instruction, or refuses to
carry out a policy or procedure well-known by the employee to be central to the
fulfilment of the employer’s objectives.
[66]

the “reprimand” to a written warning.

a)

Were these work orders?

[
116
]

The Bucks were being directed on how they were to communicate with the
board and with Oakwood Towers’ residents.  I find this to be a work order.

[
117
]

The evidence was not clear on what was being required by “agenda
discipline”.  There was some evidence regarding agendas not being provided 24
hours before board meetings.  Mr. Buck agreed that all parties discussed a need
for “agenda discipline”, and that included discipline amongst the board and the
managers.  Stavropoulos testified that this was a minor point.

[
118
]

I am not prepared to find that the direction that the board would need
“some form of agenda discipline” was a work order to its managers.

b)

Were these work orders clearly communicated?

[
119
]

Mr. Buck denied that the Bucks were directed that future communications should
be through Mrs. Buck, stating that was “100% false”.  Mr. Buck did not
specifically address the direction that they not communicate with residents
unless approved by the board.

[
120
]

If “some form of agenda discipline” was supposed to be a work order, I
find that Oakwood Towers did not clearly communicate what it meant by this
direction.

c)

Were these work orders authorized, lawful and reasonable?

[
121
]

Work orders must be authorized, lawful and reasonable.

[
122
]

The Bucks were Oakwood Towers’ resident managers.  They were both
required by the Agreement to communicate with the board, and with owners and
residents to carry out their duties under Section 4 of the Agreement.  Oakwood
Towers’ attempt to restrict communications between the board to only Mrs. Buck
interfered with Mr. Buck’s ability to carry out his duties under the Agreement.

[
123
]

Oakwood Towers’ further attempt to restrict the Bucks’ written
communications to residents unless approved by the board also interfered with
the Bucks’ abilities to carry out their duties under the Agreement.  For
example, Section 4(k) required the Bucks to communicate with “unit occupants or
owners” to discharge [their] duties” and to “apply and enforce the By-laws of
the Corporation”.

[
124
]

I find that the communication work orders directly interfered with the
Bucks’ ability to perform the services listed in Section 4 of the Agreement.
Work orders that interfere with an employee’s duties are, in my view, not
authorized.

[
125
]

Even if I am incorrect in my findings that the work orders regarding
communications were not authorized, work orders are required to be reasonable
and lawful.

[
126
]

The first communication directive was that all future communications be
through Mrs. Buck, not Mr. Buck.  Mr. Buck denied that Stavropoulos directed the
foregoing.  There is no need for me to reconcile the discrepancy between
Stavropoulos’ evidence and Mr. Buck’s evidence on this point as I find that
this work order was neither reasonable, nor lawful.  It was unreasonable as it
was based on Oakwood Towers’ acceptance of Stenzel’s complaint against Mr. Buck
without investigation.  It was unlawful because it was contrary to the Agreement
that required that both the Bucks communicate with the Oakwood Towers’ board.

[
127
]

The second communication direction was that the Bucks were not to communicate
in writing with residents unless approved by the board.  I can reasonably
infer, based on Stenzel’s December 17, 2015 email and Stavropoulos’ evidence
including his handwritten notes from the December 19, 2015 meeting, that this directive
flowed from the Bucks sending the December 11, 2015 letter to Stenzel’s 13 tenants
advising that they would no longer be managing Stenzel’s suites as the suite
management agreement had been terminated.  There was a second letter referred
to; however, it was not produced in evidence.

[
128
]

I find that this work order was neither reasonable, nor lawful.  It was
unreasonable as it was based on Stenzel’s complaints that the Bucks were
communicating with her tenants following the termination of the suite
management agreement between Stenzel and the Bucks.  The first letter dated
December 11, 2015 was a notification letter advising Stenzel’s tenants that the
Bucks were no longer managing the suites.  I have reviewed that letter.  There
is nothing inappropriate about the letter.  It was simply informational.  I
find that Oakwood Towers’ board decided to issue a ban on communications with
residents based on its acceptance of Stenzel’s uninvestigated complaint against
Mr. Buck, and based on Stenzel’s complaint that the Bucks were communicating
with her tenants following termination of the suite management agreement.
There was no evidence that there were any other issues or concerns with the
Bucks’ communications otherwise with owners or residents of Oakwood Towers at
the time.

[
129
]

It was unreasonable for the board to involve itself in a dispute between
the Bucks and Stenzel that arose from a separate contractual relationship
between the Bucks and Stenzel.  While Stenzel elevated the dispute to the board

have involved itself in the matter.  This is particularly of concern where
Stenzel sent texts to the Bucks threatening their positions as resident
managers of Oakwood Towers on December 12/13, 2015.  Oakwood Towers had no
authority to discipline or direct the Bucks with respect to issues that
originated as a result of the termination of a separate suite management
contract with Stenzel, nor was it reasonable for Oakwood Towers to do so.

[
130
]

Any failure on the part of the Bucks, as was attested to by Stavropoulos
and Stenzel, to comply with the two communication directives issued following
the December 19, 2015 board meeting attracts no consequences as the orders were
not authorized, lawful or reasonable.

d)

Was there a deliberate challenge?

[
131
]

There was no evidence that the Bucks deliberately challenged the board
in relation to the December, 2015 issues.

e)

Insubordination

[
132
]

I find there was no insubordination arising from the directions that
Oakwood Towers gave the Bucks on December 19, 2015 as the work orders were not
authorized, lawful or reasonable.  I also find that the agenda discipline
direction was too vague to constitute a work order, and it was not clearly
communicated.
There was no evidence of any deliberate
challenge to the board.

direct[ed]”
that
Mr. Buck “
cease and desist
” these types of communications”.  Stavropoulos
stated that Mr. Buck’s job as manager of Oakwood Towers was to implement the

“directed to immediately stop this conduct” and “not distract any Board members

[
179
]

Mr. Buck responded to Stavropoulos’ cease and desist email on July 6, 2016.
In his response, he raised the ongoing conflict with Stenzel, and he expressed
frustration with his perception that Stavropoulos had sided with Stenzel on

noted further that “all of the Board issues of the past and present that are

encouraged Stavropoulos “to start consistently making board decisions based on
the Bylaws and the
Condominium Property Act
”, and “to start consistently
empowering Sandra & I to carry out our duties”.  He ended his email with
“hope and trust” that Stavropoulos will choose to work with them and the entire
board in a “team environment versus working against” them.  Stavropoulos
characterized Mr. Buck’s email as “very inflammatory”.

[
180
]

Stavropoulos’ emailed reply was that his email was a “direction” in his
capacity as board President, and that he “will not give” him “another warning”.

a)

Was there a work order?

[
181
]

Oakwood Towers relies on the second July 6, 2016 email that Mr. Buck
sent to Stavropoulos and the board after Stavropolous’ July 6, 2016 cease and
desist direction as a pivotal act of insubordination, justifying termination of
the Agreement.

[
182
]

Oakwood Towers refers to
Amos v. Alberta
[102]
,
arguing that the facts in
Amos
are analogous to the facts in this case.
In
Amos
, the employee was a systems analyst who refused to carry out a
task that was within his position and job description, skill and experience.
[103]
Specifically,
the employee refused to “clean up the load library” (delete files), and he
wrote a memorandum to his employer “declining to do” the task.
[104]
I have
carefully reviewed
Amos
, and I do not find it to be a factually
analogous case.  The Bucks’ employment relationship with Oakwood Towers was
markedly different than that of the employee in
Amos
.  For example, Section
4(g) of the Agreement between the Bucks and Oakwood Towers required the Bucks
to communicate with unit occupants, owners and residents to apply and enforce
Oakwood Towers’ By-laws.

[
183
]

Oakwood Towers admitted, in its written argument, that Stavropoulos’
cease and desist direction “was not a direction to perform a job duty”.
Oakwood Towers maintains that the cease and desist direction was specific to
“these types of communications”, which Stavropoulos had called a “5 page
diatribe”.

[
184
]

I find that Stavropoulos’ direction that the Bucks cease and desist
“these types of communications” was a work order.  Section 13 of the Agreement
required the Bucks to act “in compliance with directions from the Board”.  The
Bucks were being directed on how they were to communicate with the board.

b)

Was the work order clearly communicated?

[
185
]

The work order directed the Bucks to cease and desist from “these types
of communications”.  “These types of communications” refer to Mr. Buck’s first July
6, 2016 email, which Stavropoulos described as a “5 page diatribe”.  Stavropoulos’
cease and desist direction was also aimed at what he termed Mr. Buck’s
“continuing behavior of accusations and case building against board members”.  Mr.
Buck was also “directed” not to distract board members “further on matters that
are not board business”.

[
186
]

Roberge, another Oakwood Towers’ board member, sent a reply to the Bucks
before Stavropoulos’ cease and desist direction thanking the Bucks for the same
July 6, 2016 email, and supporting the Bucks.  I can reasonably infer that she
did not find Mr. Buck’s email to be a “5 page diatribe”, nor did she appear to
be “distracted” by “matters that are not board business”.

[
187
]

It is not clear what was meant by “these types of communications”.  One
of Stavropoulos’ fellow board members Roberge thanked the Bucks for the email
that Stavropoulos characterized as a “5 page diatribe”.  If one board member was
thanking an employee for an email, and another was characterizing it as a “5
page diatribe”, how was an employee to understand what is meant by “these types
of communications”?  I find that this direction was not clear, and so it could
not be “clearly communicated”.

[
188
]

Despite that finding, I will proceed to the next step of the analysis as
Oakwood Towers relies on this work order as the pivotal act of insubordination.

c)

Was the work order authorized, lawful and reasonable?

[
189
]

Section 4 of the Agreement gave the Bucks the “authority and power” to
assist the board with managing the affairs of Oakwood Towers, to keep an
accurate register of all unit owners and tenants, to attend board meetings and
furnish all information requested by the board, to communicate with unit
occupants and owners to apply and enforce Oakwood Towers’ Bylaws, and to report
any Bylaw infractions or suspicious activity to the board.  While the Bucks
were to act “in compliance with directions from the Board”
[105]
, the board delegated
significant responsibilities to the Bucks which required communications with
the board, owners and residents.

[
190
]

I have reviewed Mr. Buck’s first July 6, 2016 email.  I disagree with
Stavropoulos’ characterization of it as a “5 page diatribe”.  I disagree with
Stavropoulos’ suggestion that it was “interspersed” with “a number of very
insolent comments”.  While Mr. Buck expressed frustration with his interactions
with Stenzel and with a perceived lack of support from Stavropoulos, Mr. Buck’s
email explained why Stenzel’s tenant’s vehicle was towed, and his email
detailed the circumstances that lead up to the action including both Stenzel’s
failure to respond to him, and her tenant’s refusal to identify himself.
Section 4(l) of the Agreement required Mr. Buck to report Bylaw infractions and
suspicious activity to the board.  Section 4(k) permitted him to enforce
Oakwood Towers’ bylaws which is what he did when he had the vehicle towed.
Stenzel had threatened the Bucks by demanding $500.00 for towing (“or I will be
taking further action to collect”).  I find that Mr. Buck’s email of July 6,
2016 provided a report to the board of the circumstances under which the
vehicle had been towed as he was required to do in Section 4(l).  I find that
Stavropoulos’ direction that Mr. Buck not provide such reports to the board was
not authorized as it was contrary to Section 4 of the Agreement.

[
191
]

Even if I am incorrect in finding that the work order was not
authorized, work orders are required to be reasonable and lawful.

[
192
]

The cease and desist communication work order was neither reasonable,
nor lawful.  Stavropoulos and Oakwood Towers did not conduct an investigation
into the towing incident.  Stavropoulos rejected Mr. Buck’s attempt to address
the matter, and he accused Mr. Buck of “continuing behaviour” of “accusations
and case building against board members”.  There was no evidence of “continuing
behaviour” of “accusations and case building” on the part of Mr. Buck.  The
July, 2016 issue arose as a result of Stenzel’s July 1, 2016 email to the board
where she called into question Mr. Buck’s experience and ability, and she
demanded that Oakwood Towers’ resident manager pay her $500.00.  Stenzel
elevated this issue to the board level by sending her email to the board.  The
Bucks were not afforded a fair and reasonable opportunity to respond to
Stenzel’s accusations.  Oakwood Towers owed a duty to the Bucks to deal with
them in good faith and fairly
[106]
,
and it is questionable whether it discharged its duty.   I find that Oakwood
Towers’ accusation that the Bucks were guilty of inappropriate “behaviour” and
“conduct” was unreasonable in the circumstances, and I further find that
Oakwood Towers’ banning of further communication with the board based on
uninvestigated and unsupported allegations was likewise unreasonable, and
unlawful.

[
193
]

Despite finding that the cease and desist work order was unauthorized,
unreasonable and unlawful, I will proceed to the next step of the analysis as
Oakwood Towers relies on this work order as its pivotal act of insubordination.

d)

Was this work order disobeyed?  Was that disobedience deliberate and
intentional?

[
194
]

Oakwood Towers says that Mr. Buck disobeyed Stavropoulos’ cease and
desist work order when Mr. Buck sent his second July 6, 2016 email.  Oakwood
Towers argues that the mere fact the Mr. Buck replied to Stavropoulos was
willful disobedience sufficient make out insubordination.

[
195
]

Mr. Buck’s second email expressed frustration.  Stavropoulos characterized
the second email as “inflammatory”.  I disagree.  Mr. Buck’s email was sent
with “hope and trust” that they can work together as a “team”, and he
encouraged Stavropoulos to support he and Mrs. Buck in carrying out their
duties under the Agreement.  Oakwood Towers’ employees not feeling supported by
the board is “board business”.  Oakwood Towers’ employees feeling “intimidated”
and “bullied” is also “board business”.  As the Bucks’ employer, Oakwood Towers
was subject to a broad duty of good faith and fair dealing.
[107]

[
196
]

I find that Mr. Buck’s second email of July 6, 2016 did not constitute
disobedience of the cease and desist work order.  Mr. Buck’s second email
addressed matters of board business, and the work order did not prohibit him
from communicating with the board regarding such matters.

[
197
]

Despite finding that the cease and desist work order was not disobeyed
by the Bucks, I will proceed to the next step of the analysis as Oakwood Towers
relies on this work order as its pivotal act of insubordination.

d)         Was the disobedience
grave or very serious?

[
198
]

Oakwood Towers relies on Stavropoulos’ evidence on this issue, alleging
that the Bucks’ alleged disobedience was very serious, and that it alone
constituted just cause for termination of the Agreement.  This requires me to
assess both credibility and reliability.  Stavropoulos’ evidence devolved into
complaints unrelated to the cease and desist work order, and unrelated to the
question of whether Oakwood Towers can establish insubordination based on the
Bucks’ alleged disobedience of the same.

[
199
]

Stavropoulos testified that this “event” was “so significant”, from his
perspective, because it was a “culmination of 10 months of unacceptable
conduct”.  There was no evidence that there had been “10 months of unacceptable
conduct”.   I was referred to the incidents in September, 2015; December, 2015;
January, 2016; June, 2016 and July, 2016, all of which I have dealt with in
these Reasons.

[
200
]

Stavropoulos testified further that there had been a “heaping of one
email after another”
[108]
.
This is similar to his accusation that Mr. Buck provided an “evidence email”
when he responded to Roberge’s request for further information.  There was no
evidence of a “heaping” of emails as described by Stavropoulos.

[
201
]

Over the course of time, Stavropoulos claimed that the “same issues kept
getting raised by the Bucks” and “elevated to the board level which
effectively” “hi-jacked” the board’s agenda because they were no longer dealing
with board business, but rather the board was forced to deal “with this
avalanche of accusations”, and “irrational conclusions”.   Stavropoulos
acknowledged that he “permitted” the interpersonal dispute
[109]
between Mr. Buck
and Stenzel to be brought to the board level in December, 2015 as he was
“seeking resolution” of the same (although he recognized it was not board business).
Stavropoulos did not acknowledge that Stenzel (as opposed to the Bucks)
elevated the December, 2015 and the July, 2016 issues to the board level
through her emails to the board.  He had difficulty acknowledging that it was
not appropriate to suggest that the Bucks “hi-jacked” the board’s agenda when
the complaints originated with Stenzel and when he permitted the complaints to
be discussed at the board level.

[
202
]

Stavropoulos testified that the “issues that were created by Mr. Buck”
“related specifically” to that interpersonal dispute.  The issue was
done
[110]
“from his
perspective”.  He further testified that the board “reached a boiling point”
because of a parking issue that originated in December, 2015 that took up the entire
July, 2016 board meeting.  The evidence was that the December, 2015 issue arose
from termination of the suite management agreement between the Bucks and
Stenzel, not from any parking issue.  Stavropoulos failed to recognize that
Stenzel as opposed to Mr. Buck “created” the “issues” related to the
interpersonal dispute by repeatedly bringing those issues to the board.  While
he suggested that the issue was “done” from his perspective, the evidence is
that Oakwood Towers never resolved the issue.  Instead, they reprimanded the

[
203
]

Stavropoulos claimed that he asked Mr. Buck whether Oakwood Towers was
insured at the July 5, 2016 board meeting.  He alleged that Mr. Buck was
“evasive” and “refused to answer” his question.  He asserted that he was
“absolutely floored” and characterized Mr. Buck as “obstructionist”.  I have
reviewed Stavropoulos’ handwritten notes from the July 5, 2016 meeting.  His

responding to Mr. Buck’s concern about a lack of funds to pay the insurance
stating: “In terms of the insurance payment, that payment will need to be
deferred to July, once we have been invoiced for it and after that month’s
condo fee payments have been deposited”.  Stavropoulos’ testimony was
inconsistent with the documentary evidence as Mr. Buck, not Stavropoulos, was
concerned about lack of funds for payment of the insurance premium.

[
204
]

Stavropoulos stated that the July 5, 2016 meeting was an “absolute
disaster”, and repeated that it was a “culmination of events where they were
completely paralyzed”.  He pointed to:

•

“38 uncompleted action items” from previous board meetings
[111]
; and

•

A “massive dispute” with respect to a parking issue that
originated in December, 2015.

[
205
]

I have reviewed the Minutes from May 13, 2014 to December 1, 2015.  Many
of the outstanding tasks were tasks to be completed by Oakwood Towers’ lawyers,
Stenzel and other board members.  Some involved creating a “garden committee”.
One outstanding task was the receipt of Minutes from Stavropoulos in October,
2015.    Based on review of the Minutes, I do not accept that there were 38

counted 18, with the board also having 18 outstanding action items, and Stenzel

I have already addressed the Stavropoulos’ allegation that the “parking issue”
had continued from December, 2015.

[
206
]

While the board meeting may have been an “absolute disaster”, I do not
accept that the board was “completely paralyzed”.  The Minutes of the board
meetings that were produced in evidence confirm that the board was able to
carry out its business.

[
207
]

Stavropoulos stated that “we were done” on that basis alone.  It is not
clear who “we” were.  I can reasonably infer from the following statement that
Stavropoulos was “done” as he reiterated that he did not need the manager “to
tell” him or the board “how to run our building”, and that “it goes the other
direction”.

[
208
]

Stavropoulos’ evidence here digressed from the cease and desist work
order.  His evidence was focused on the July 5, 2016 board meeting.  Oakwood
Towers does not rely on anything that occurred at that board meeting in support
of its insubordination allegation against the Bucks.  Instead, they rely on Mr.
Buck’s second email of July 6, 2016 in support of their pivotal allegation of
insubordination.  This calls into question the basis of Oakwood Towers’
insubordination case against the Bucks.

[
209
]

In Paragraphs 23 and 24, I outlined the factors that I am required to
take into account to assess credibility and reliability.  I had the following issues
with Stavropoulos’ evidence:

•

He denied giving legal advice to Oakwood Towers, but he was
cross-examined on March 6, 2017 board meeting where he initially agreed that he
attended by telephone, but then denied that he attended and made the comments
[112]
reflected in the
Minutes arising from the board meeting;

•

He assumed that there was tension between Mr. Buck and the
roofing contractor without seeing any of the communications between them;

•

He accepted Stenzel’s report of a lien threat from the roofing
company without corroborating the veracity of the same;

•

He characterized Mr. Buck’s reply to a fellow board member as an
“evidence email”;

•

He suggested that Mr. Buck has some sort of “mentality” in “how
he dealt with contractors and suppliers” when the evidence was that Mr. Buck
communicated professionally and politely with such contractors;

•

He repeatedly referred to the reserve fund transfer in January,
2016 as “the Bucks’ decision” despite evidence that the same was approved and
effected by a fellow board member;

•

He referred to the reserve fund transfer in January, 2016 as
being “effected” by the Bucks when it was “effected” by Bigelow;

•

He along with other board members contemplated termination as
early as January, 2016 where there was no just cause;

•

He alleged that there were “communication problems” and
“tensions” not supported by the evidence;

•

He claimed that a board special resolution was required to
transfer funds from the reserve to operations accounts when they were
automatically linked to do so;

•

He blamed the Bucks for the January, 2016 reserve fund transfer
that Bigelow approved and effected, and that would have happened in any event
as a result of the linking of the accounts;

•

He testified that an altercation occurred between Stenzel and the
Bucks in July, 2016 when there was no other evidence of that;

•

He repeatedly claimed that the Bucks elevated these issues to the
board level when the evidence was that Stenzel was the one who did so, and he
permitted non-board business to be so elevated;

•

He made allegations against the Bucks which were unsupported
otherwise in the evidence as have already been enumerated in this decision; and

•

He repeatedly negatively characterized the Bucks’ motivations,
emotional state (ie. “irrational”, “avalanche”, etc.

[
210
]

Based on the foregoing, I find Stavropoulos’ evidence on these critical
issues not to be reliable.  His evidence was not given in an objective fashion,
it was not fair and balanced, and it was inconsistent with other evidence
entered at trial.  I am not able to rely on Stavropoulos’ evidence, particularly
as it relates to Oakwood Towers’ allegations that the Bucks were engaging in
misconduct, and further, as it relates to just cause.

[
211
]

Even if I am incorrect in my finding that the cease and desist work order
was not disobeyed by the Bucks, I do not accept that Mr. Buck’s sending of the
second July 6, 2016 email to the board was “grave or very serious”
disobedience. The second email was sent with “hope and trust” that they could
work together as a “team”, and Mr. Buck encouraged Stavropoulos to support the
Bucks in carrying out their duties under the Agreement.

[
212
]

Despite my findings in this section, I will proceed to the next step of
the analysis as Oakwood Towers relies on this work order as its pivotal act of
insubordination.

e)

Did the employee understand s/he would be terminated if s/he disobeyed
the order? / Was the employee made aware unequivocally that discipline was the
penalty for disobedience?

[
213
]

Even if I am incorrect in my earlier findings, there are no consequences
outlined in either Stavropoulos’ cease and desist work order, or the final
warning email that followed.

[
214
]

Oakwood Towers did not state that discipline would be the penalty for
disobedience.  Oakwood Towers further did not state that the Bucks would be
terminated if they disobeyed Stavropolous’ cease and desist direction.  Mr.
Buck’s second email of July 6, 2016 does not reflect any understanding that he
would be terminated for disobeying Stavropoulos’ cease and desist email as he
notes hope that the issues can be resolved in the future.

[
215
]

I find that Oakwood Towers failed to make the Bucks aware that
discipline or termination would the penalty for disobedience.

f)

Was there a deliberate challenge?

[
216
]

I find that the emails that Mr. Buck sent to Stavropoulos and the board
on July 6, 2016 were not a deliberate challenge for the reasons noted in my
analysis set out in this section.

[
217
]

In
Kokilev v. Picquic Tool Company Inc.
[113]
, the court noted
that disagreeing with an employer’s “point of view does not give rise to a
conflict of interest, a breach of fiduciary duty, or for that matter just cause
to terminate for disobedience or insubordination”
[114]
.  It requires “a
lot more”
[115]
.
The Court noted:

“… It would be astounding if the law held that a
management or key employee was not permitted to express a contrary view to the
president of a corporation during a meeting with other key employees, but may
do so only in a private meeting with the president…”
[116]

[
218
]

I find that the Bucks were entitled to express a contrary opinion to
that of Stavropoulos.  I find, to the extent that they did so in the either the
first or second July 6, 2016 email, that they were not guilty of any
insubordination in doing so.

g)

Insubordination

[
219
]

I find there was no insubordination arising from the communications that
Mr. Buck sent to Stavropoulos on July 6, 2016 for the reasons outlined above.

I.

Notice of Termination Inconsistent with Just Cause

[
220
]

The Board convened a special meeting on July 8, 2016 to discuss the
Bucks’ Agreement with Oakwood Towers.  Stavropoulos made a motion to terminate
the Bucks’ Agreement, which was seconded by Stenzel.  That motion was passed.

[
221
]

Stavropoulos drafted the termination letter that was emailed to the
Bucks on July 15, 2016.  The termination letter indicates that Oakwood Towers
resolved to terminate the management agreement “in accordance with section 13
of the management agreement on account of your continued and escalating
insubordination”.

[
222
]

The board further resolved to continue to pay the monthly gross salary
up to and including July 31, 2016 based on the three conditions outlined in the
termination letter including requiring the Bucks to cooperate with the new
management company; directing the Bucks not to correspond with building owners
or residents, third-party suppliers or contractors with respect to the change;
and directing the Bucks to remain positive and helpful during the transition.

[
223
]

Oakwood Towers’ termination letter, therefore, provided the Bucks with
two weeks’ working notice on the conditions outlined therein.  The Bucks say
that the two weeks’ notice period was inconsistent with just cause.

[
224
]

Just
cause requires a finding of misconduct such that the employment relationship
can no longer viably exist.  Here, the employment relationship continued for
two weeks after termination.  The Bucks continued to carry out their duties as
managers until matters were transitioned over to the new property manager.  The
Bucks paid Oakwood Towers’ bills to the end of July, 2016.  The facts here do
not support the allegation made by Oakwood Towers that the conduct alleged was
serious enough to repudiate the employment contract.

[
225
]

I agree with the Bucks that the two weeks’ notice period was
inconsistent with just cause, and I make that finding.

J.

Mr. Buck or Mrs. Buck’s Alleged Insubordination

[
226
]

One
of the issues that arose during the trial was whether the alleged
insubordination was that of Mr. Buck alone, or Mr. and Mrs. Buck together.  If
the alleged insubordination was only that of Mr. Buck, the question raised was
whether that insubordination provided grounds for terminating the entire
Agreement, or whether that insubordination only provided grounds for
terminating the Agreement with Mr. Buck.

[
227
]

I
do not have to decide that issue as I have found that there was no
insubordination on the part of either Mr. or Mrs. Buck.

K.

Conclusion

[
228
]

I
have carefully assessed the nature and extent of the alleged misconduct as
required in
McKinley
.
[117]

I find there was no insubordination on the part of the Bucks, whether that
insubordination be a willful and deliberate disobedience of a work order, or
behaviour that is a deliberate challenge.   Based on those findings, I do not
need to consider the second and third factors in the
McKinley
[118]

framework
[119]
.

[
229
]

I
find that Oakwood Towers wrongfully terminated the Agreement with the Bucks
without cause, and without being able to establish insubordination on a balance

V.

WHAT DAMAGES ARE THE BUCKS ENTITLED TO FOR WRONGFUL TERMINATION
OF THE AGREEMENT?

A.

Fixed Term Employment Contract/Obligation to Mitigate

[
230
]

The
Agreement was an employment contract with a term of May 1, 2014 to August 31,
2017.  I find that the Agreement was a fixed term contract.  The Bucks were
wrongfully terminated on July 31, 2016.

[
231
]

Employees
bound by fixed term contracts are entitled to judgment for the full contractual
amount
[120]
.
An employer who dismisses an employee before a fixed term contract has expired
must pay the dismissed employee the salary s/he would have received had s/he
worked until the end date
[121]
.
There is no obligation on the employee in a fixed term contract to mitigate his
or her damages (where the amount in question is either liquidated damages or a
contractual sum)
[122]
.

[
232
]

Mitigation
was not addressed by Oakwood Towers at trial.  Oakwood Towers failed to
establish any evidence of any mitigation principles which might assist them
[123]
.

[
233
]

My
view is that the Bucks has no duty to mitigate, and they are entitled to be
paid the salaries that they would have received, had they worked until August
31, 2017.

).

C.

Separate Counterclaims

[

solicitor-client costs be awarded in their favour, particularly arising from
Oakwood Towers’ fraud allegations against them.  The Bucks rely on
